[Level 4 · Models & learning]{.level-4} [⏱ ~80 min]{} [Prerequisites: [Proportions and the chi-square test](../08-inference/35-proportions-chisq.qmd), [Principal component analysis](50-pca.qmd)]{}

::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- describe a contingency table through **row and column profiles**, **masses** and **inertia** ($\chi^2 / n$);
- explain correspondence analysis (CA) as a "PCA for tables" and run it with `ca::ca()`;
- distinguish **standard and principal coordinates** and draw a correct **symmetric map**;
- use **contributions** and **quality of representation (cos²)** to decide what a map can tell you;
- interpret a CA map without the usual mistakes.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ca)
```

## 1. Why correspondence analysis?

In [Proportions and the chi-square test](../08-inference/35-proportions-chisq.qmd) you learnt to ask *"are hair colour and eye colour associated?"* The chi-square test answers yes or no. But it does not say **which** hair colours go with **which** eye colours, nor how the categories relate to each other.

Correspondence analysis (CA) turns a contingency table into a **map**: categories with similar profiles are drawn close together, and the main patterns of association become directions on the map. It is to a table of counts what PCA is to a table of measurements.

## 2. The data and the chi-square test

`HairEyeColor` cross-classifies 592 students by hair colour, eye colour and sex. We collapse over sex:

```{r}
#| label: table
hair_eye <- margin.table(HairEyeColor, margin = c(1, 2))
hair_eye

chi <- chisq.test(hair_eye)
chi
```

The test gives $\chi^2 =$ `r round(chi$statistic, 1)` with `r chi$parameter` degrees of freedom ($(4-1)(4-1)$): overwhelming evidence of association. The **Pearson residuals** (observed − expected) / √expected show where the association lies:

```{r}
#| label: residuals
round(chi$residuals, 1)
```

Large positive residuals (Blond–Blue, Black–Brown) mark combinations that occur much more often than independence would predict. CA will summarise this whole table of residuals in a picture.

## 3. Profiles, masses and inertia

CA works with **proportions**, not counts.

- A **row profile** is a row divided by its total: the distribution of eye colours *within* one hair colour.
- The **average row profile** (the column margins) is the distribution of eye colours in the whole sample.

```{r}
#| label: profiles
round(prop.table(hair_eye, margin = 1), 2)    # row profiles
round(prop.table(margin.table(hair_eye, 2)), 2)  # average profile
```

Blond-haired students have a very different profile from the average (`r round(100 * prop.table(hair_eye, 1)["Blond", "Blue"])`% blue eyes versus `r round(100 * prop.table(margin.table(hair_eye, 2))["Blue"])`% overall), while brown-haired students are close to the average.

- The **mass** of a row is its share of the total ($n_{i+}/n$). Heavy rows (many people) weigh more in the analysis.
- The **inertia** of a table measures how far the profiles are, on average, from the average profile. It equals

$$
\text{total inertia} = \frac{\chi^2}{n}.
$$

```{r}
#| label: inertia
n <- sum(hair_eye)
unname(chi$statistic / n)
```

If hair and eye colour were independent, every row profile would equal the average profile and the inertia would be 0. CA decomposes this inertia into **dimensions**, just as PCA decomposes variance into components.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: chi-square distances

The distance between a row profile $a_i$ and the average profile $c$ is the **chi-square distance**

$$
d^2(a_i, c) = \sum_j \frac{(a_{ij} - c_j)^2}{c_j}.
$$

Dividing by $c_j$ gives more weight to differences in **rare** columns. The total inertia is the mass-weighted average of these squared distances: $\sum_i r_i \, d^2(a_i, c) = \chi^2/n$, where $r_i$ is the row mass. The same holds for columns.
:::

## 4. Running CA

```{r}
#| label: ca-fit
ca_he <- ca(hair_eye)
ca_he
```

A 4 × 4 table has at most $\min(4, 4) - 1 = 3$ dimensions. The **principal inertias** (eigenvalues) are the squared singular values:

```{r}
#| label: inertia-dims
eig <- ca_he$sv^2
data.frame(dim = seq_along(eig),
           inertia = round(eig, 4),
           percent = round(100 * eig / sum(eig), 1),
           cumulative = round(100 * cumsum(eig) / sum(eig), 1))
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- The inertias add up to the total inertia: `r round(sum(eig), 4)` = $\chi^2/n$.
- **Dimension 1** alone accounts for `r round(100 * eig[1] / sum(eig), 1)`% of the inertia, **dimension 2** for `r round(100 * eig[2] / sum(eig), 1)`%. Together, a two-dimensional map shows `r round(100 * sum(eig[1:2]) / sum(eig), 1)`% of the association in the table — almost all of it.
:::

## 5. Standard versus principal coordinates

This is the point where most mistakes happen, so let's be careful. `ca()` returns **standard coordinates** in `rowcoord` and `colcoord`. Each dimension of standard coordinates has (weighted) variance 1 — they do **not** reflect how important the dimension is.

**Principal coordinates** are standard coordinates multiplied by the singular value of each dimension:

$$
\text{principal} = \text{standard} \times \sqrt{\text{inertia of the dimension}}.
$$

In principal coordinates, the spread of the points along each axis reflects the inertia of that axis, and the distances between rows (or between columns) approximate their chi-square distances.

```{r}
#| label: coords
row_pc <- sweep(ca_he$rowcoord, 2, ca_he$sv, `*`)   # principal coordinates
col_pc <- sweep(ca_he$colcoord, 2, ca_he$sv, `*`)
round(row_pc[, 1:2], 3)
round(col_pc[, 1:2], 3)
```

The **symmetric map** — the standard CA plot — shows **both rows and columns in principal coordinates**. That is what `plot()` draws by default:

```{r}
#| label: fig-ca-plot
#| fig-cap: "Symmetric CA map of hair colour (blue) and eye colour (red), both in principal coordinates."
plot(ca_he, map = "symmetric")
```

The same map with ggplot:

```{r}
#| label: fig-ca-gg
#| fig-cap: "Symmetric CA map built from principal coordinates. Axis labels show the percentage of inertia."
pct <- round(100 * eig / sum(eig), 1)

ca_map <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(label = ca_he$rownames, dim1 = row_pc[, 1], dim2 = row_pc[, 2],
             type = "Hair"),
  data.frame(label = ca_he$colnames, dim1 = col_pc[, 1], dim2 = col_pc[, 2],
             type = "Eye")
)

ggplot(ca_map, aes(dim1, dim2, colour = type, shape = type)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), vjust = -0.9, show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = paste0("Dimension 1 (", pct[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("Dimension 2 (", pct[2], "%)"),
       colour = NULL, shape = NULL)
```

`coord_equal()` matters: one unit on each axis must have the same length, otherwise distances on the map are distorted.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: CA as an SVD of standardised residuals

Let $P = N/n$ be the table of proportions, $r$ and $c$ the row and column masses, and $D_r = \mathrm{diag}(r)$, $D_c = \mathrm{diag}(c)$. CA is the singular value decomposition of the matrix of **standardised residuals**

$$
S = D_r^{-1/2}\,(P - r c^\top)\,D_c^{-1/2} = U \Sigma V^\top .
$$

Each element of $S$ is a Pearson residual divided by $\sqrt n$, so $\sum_{ij} s_{ij}^2 = \chi^2/n$, and the squared singular values $\sigma_k^2$ are the principal inertias. Then

- standard coordinates: rows $D_r^{-1/2} U$, columns $D_c^{-1/2} V$;
- principal coordinates: rows $D_r^{-1/2} U \Sigma$, columns $D_c^{-1/2} V \Sigma$.

We can verify it by hand:

```{r}
#| label: svd-by-hand
P  <- hair_eye / n
rm <- rowSums(P)
cm <- colSums(P)
S  <- diag(1 / sqrt(rm)) %*% (P - rm %o% cm) %*% diag(1 / sqrt(cm))
s  <- svd(S)

s$d[1:3]^2                                # principal inertias
ca_he$sv^2                                # same, from ca()
all.equal(abs(diag(1 / sqrt(rm)) %*% s$u[, 1:3]),
          abs(unname(ca_he$rowcoord)))    # standard row coordinates
```

(As in PCA, the sign of each dimension is arbitrary, so we compare absolute values.)
:::

## 6. Reading the map correctly

In a symmetric map, use these rules:

1. **Distances among rows** (hair colours) approximate the chi-square distances between their profiles: hair colours close together have similar eye-colour distributions. The same holds **among columns**.
2. **Distance from the origin**: the origin is the average profile. Categories far from the origin have profiles very different from the average; categories near the origin are "average".
3. **Row–column relationships** are read through **directions**, not distances: a row and a column that lie in the **same direction from the origin**, both far from it, are positively associated (more frequent together than expected); opposite directions mean they co-occur less than expected.
4. **Distances between a row point and a column point are not directly interpretable** in a symmetric map. The two sets of points are on different scales. (The *asymmetric* maps, `plot(ca_he, map = "rowprincipal")`, allow a stricter reading of row–column relations, at the cost of a less compact picture.)

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## What the hair–eye map shows

- **Dimension 1** (`r pct[1]`%) is a light–dark axis. **Blond** hair and **blue** eyes lie together at one end; **black** and, less extremely, brown hair lie with **brown** eyes at the other. This matches the largest residuals: Blond–Blue (`r round(chi$residuals["Blond", "Blue"], 1)`) and Black–Brown (`r round(chi$residuals["Black", "Brown"], 1)`).
- **Dimension 2** (`r pct[2]`%) separates **red** hair and **green** (and partly hazel) eyes from black hair (residual Red–Green: `r round(chi$residuals["Red", "Green"], 1)`).
- **Brown** hair is close to the origin: its eye-colour profile is close to the average, as we saw in the profiles.
:::

Avoid reading quadrants as categories ("quadrant I = …"): the axes' signs are arbitrary and the quadrants have no meaning in themselves.

## 7. Contributions and quality of representation

Two diagnostics help you decide which points drive a dimension and which points are faithfully shown.

- The **contribution** of a row to a dimension is the share of that dimension's inertia due to the row: $\text{mass} \times (\text{standard coordinate})^2$. Contributions to each dimension add up to 1.
- The **quality** of representation of a row on a dimension (**cos²**) is the share of the row's own inertia that the dimension shows: $(\text{principal coordinate})^2 / (\text{chi-square distance to the centroid})^2$. Summed over dimensions 1 and 2 it tells you how well the point is represented on the map (1 = perfectly).

```{r}
#| label: ctr-cos2
row_ctr  <- ca_he$rowmass * ca_he$rowcoord[, 1:2]^2
row_cos2 <- row_pc[, 1:2]^2 / ca_he$rowdist^2
col_ctr  <- ca_he$colmass * ca_he$colcoord[, 1:2]^2
col_cos2 <- col_pc[, 1:2]^2 / ca_he$coldist^2

round(cbind(ctr = row_ctr, cos2 = row_cos2, quality = rowSums(row_cos2)), 3)
round(cbind(ctr = col_ctr, cos2 = col_cos2, quality = rowSums(col_cos2)), 3)
```

`summary()` reports the same quantities, multiplied by 1000 (per mille):

```{r}
#| label: summary-ca
summary(ca_he)
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read `summary()`

- `mass` — share of the total; `qlt` — quality of representation in the dimensions shown (sum of cos²); `inr` — share of the total inertia due to this point.
- For each dimension `k`: the principal coordinate, `cor` (cos², quality on that dimension) and `ctr` (contribution to the dimension).
- Dimension 1 is mainly driven by **Blond** (contribution `r round(1000 * row_ctr["Blond", 1])`‰) and, among eye colours, by **Blue** and **Brown** (`r round(1000 * col_ctr["Blue", 1])` and `r round(1000 * col_ctr["Brown", 1])`‰). Dimension 2 is driven by **Red** hair and **Green** eyes.
- All points are well represented on the 2-D map; the weakest is **`r names(which.min(c(rowSums(row_cos2), rowSums(col_cos2))))`** (quality `r round(min(c(rowSums(row_cos2), rowSums(col_cos2))), 2)`), which still has part of its inertia on dimension 3.
:::

A point with **low quality** should not be interpreted from its position on the map: it may look close to another point only because the difference between them lies in a dimension that is not shown.

## 8. Beyond two variables: multiple correspondence analysis

With **more than two** categorical variables (e.g. hair, eye *and* sex, or the answers to a whole survey), use **multiple correspondence analysis** (MCA). MCA needs one row per individual:

```{r}
#| label: mca
#| eval: false
he_df <- as.data.frame(HairEyeColor)
people <- he_df[rep(seq_len(nrow(he_df)), he_df$Freq), c("Hair", "Eye", "Sex")]

mca_fit <- FactoMineR::MCA(people, graph = FALSE)
plot(mca_fit, invisible = "ind")    # show only the categories
```

(Not run here; it requires the **FactoMineR** package.) The reading rules are the same as for CA, but the percentages of inertia in MCA are known to be pessimistic, so they should not be compared with those of simple CA.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Plotting standard coordinates** (`rowcoord`, `colcoord`) as if they were the map. Multiply by the singular values (principal coordinates), or use `plot(ca_obj)`.
2. **Interpreting the distance between a row point and a column point** in a symmetric map. Read row–column associations through directions from the origin.
3. **Interpreting quadrants** or the sign of an axis. Signs are arbitrary.
4. **Interpreting badly represented points** (low quality / cos²) from their map position.
5. **Calling "contributions" what are in fact coordinates** — contributions are mass × standard coordinate², and they add up to 1 per dimension.
6. **Clustering CA coordinates without a reason.** CA is descriptive; if you want groups of categories, say why and use the chi-square distances, not an arbitrary algorithm on a handful of points.
:::

## 9. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. A 5 × 3 table has total inertia 0.10 and n = 500. What was the chi-square statistic, and how many CA dimensions are there?

$\chi^2 = 0.10 \times 500 = 50$. There are $\min(5, 3) - 1 = 2$ dimensions.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. On a symmetric map the point "Red hair" is very close to the point "Hazel eyes". Can you conclude that red-haired people mostly have hazel eyes?

No. Row-to-column **distances** are not interpretable in a symmetric map. Look at directions from the origin, at the residuals or at the row profile of red hair (where in fact brown eyes are the most frequent).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. What is the difference between standard and principal coordinates?

Principal coordinates = standard coordinates × singular value. Principal coordinates reflect the importance (inertia) of each dimension and approximate chi-square distances; standard coordinates have unit weighted variance on each dimension.
:::

## 10. Exercises

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — predict, then check.** Collapse `HairEyeColor` to the **Hair × Sex** table. (a) How many CA dimensions will it have? (b) Compute its total inertia as $\chi^2/n$. (c) What percentage of inertia will dimension 1 explain?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
hair_sex <- margin.table(HairEyeColor, c(1, 3))
unname(chisq.test(hair_sex)$statistic / sum(hair_sex))   # about 0.0135
ca(hair_sex)$sv^2
```
(a) $\min(4, 2) - 1 = 1$ dimension. (b) About 0.0135 — far smaller than for hair × eye (≈ 0.23): sex and hair colour are only weakly associated. (c) With a single dimension it explains 100% of the inertia.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — debug the map.** This code draws a "CA map" for `hair_eye`. What is wrong with it, and how do you fix it?

```r
ca_he <- ca(hair_eye)
plot(rbind(ca_he$rowcoord[, 1:2], ca_he$colcoord[, 1:2]), type = "n")
text(ca_he$rowcoord[, 1:2], ca_he$rownames, col = "blue")
text(ca_he$colcoord[, 1:2], ca_he$colnames, col = "red")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
It plots **standard** coordinates, which give both dimensions the same spread although dimension 1 has about nine times more inertia than dimension 2. The axes are also not on the same scale. Use principal coordinates and an aspect ratio of 1:
```r
rp <- sweep(ca_he$rowcoord[, 1:2], 2, ca_he$sv[1:2], `*`)
cp <- sweep(ca_he$colcoord[, 1:2], 2, ca_he$sv[1:2], `*`)
plot(rbind(rp, cp), type = "n", asp = 1)
text(rp, ca_he$rownames, col = "blue")
text(cp, ca_he$colnames, col = "red")
```
or simply `plot(ca_he)`.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — contributions by hand.** For the hair–eye CA, verify that (a) the contributions of the four hair colours to dimension 1 add up to 1; (b) the principal inertia of dimension 1 equals the mass-weighted sum of the squared principal coordinates of the rows.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
sum(ca_he$rowmass * ca_he$rowcoord[, 1]^2)              # 1
row_pc <- ca_he$rowcoord[, 1] * ca_he$sv[1]
c(sum(ca_he$rowmass * row_pc^2), ca_he$sv[1]^2)         # equal, about 0.209
```
Standard coordinates are normalised so that their weighted sum of squares is 1 on every dimension; multiplying by the singular value rescales it to the dimension's inertia.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — interpret.** In the summary of the hair–eye CA, `Hazel` has the lowest quality on the 2-D map, with part of its inertia (about 12%) on dimension 3. What does this imply for statements such as "hazel eyes are halfway between brown and green eyes"?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Part of what distinguishes the hazel profile is not visible in the plane of dimensions 1–2. Its position on the map is still informative (its quality is fairly high, about 0.88), but fine statements about its exact position relative to other points should be made cautiously. Check `qlt` before interpreting a point, and look at dimension 3 (`plot(ca_he, dim = c(1, 3))`) if needed.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — mini-analysis.** The `smoke` data in the **ca** package cross-classify 193 employees of a fictitious company by staff group (senior/junior managers and employees, secretaries) and smoking intensity. (a) Run a chi-square test. (b) Run CA and report the percentage of inertia of the first two dimensions. (c) Draw the symmetric map and describe the main pattern. (d) What does the chi-square test result suggest about how much to trust that pattern?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
data(smoke, package = "ca")
chisq.test(smoke)           # warning: some expected counts are small
ca_smoke <- ca(smoke)
round(100 * ca_smoke$sv^2 / sum(ca_smoke$sv^2), 1)
plot(ca_smoke)
summary(ca_smoke)
```
The test gives $\chi^2 \approx 16.4$ with 12 df, p ≈ 0.17: **no significant association**, and R warns that some expected counts are small. CA still runs: dimension 1 explains about 88% of the inertia and opposes non-smokers (with senior employees, SE, and secretaries, SC) to smokers (with junior groups, JM and JE). But with so little evidence of association overall, this pattern is a **description of this sample** that may not replicate. CA is descriptive; it does not replace the test.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Idea / function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `margin.table(x, c(1, 2))` | collapse a multi-way table to two variables |
| `prop.table(tab, 1)` | row profiles |
| $\chi^2 / n$ | total inertia: how far the profiles are from independence |
| `ca(tab)` | correspondence analysis (`sv`, `rowcoord`, `colcoord`, masses, distances) |
| `ca_obj$sv^2` | principal inertias (eigenvalues) |
| standard × `sv` | principal coordinates |
| `plot(ca_obj)` | symmetric map (both sets in principal coordinates) |
| `summary(ca_obj)` | mass, quality, inertia, coordinates, cos², contributions (×1000) |
| `FactoMineR::MCA()` | multiple CA for several categorical variables |

- CA decomposes the **inertia** $\chi^2/n$ of a table into a few dimensions.
- A correct symmetric map uses **principal coordinates** for rows and columns, with equal axis scales.
- Interpret distances **among rows** and **among columns**; read row–column association through **directions from the origin**.
- Use **contributions** to name the dimensions and **quality (cos²)** to decide which points can be interpreted.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Further reading

- Greenacre, M., *Correspondence Analysis in Practice* (3rd ed.), CRC Press — the standard practical introduction.
- Nenadić, O. & Greenacre, M. (2007), "Correspondence Analysis in R, with Two- and Three-dimensional Graphics: The ca Package", *Journal of Statistical Software* 20(3), <https://www.jstatsoft.org/v20/i03/>
:::
